# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–20 (Complete – Updated 144)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Winter of fifth year** (Chapter 20). Summer 1816: Sir Pitt (elder) dies; Pitt becomes Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet, MP. Spring 1816: Rebecca delivers son (Rawdon minor); Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton; moves into Miss Crawley's house; Lady Southdown assumes control; Miss Crawley dies. **Chapter 18 events (Summer 1816)**: Sir Pitt nearly eighty, afflicted with lumbago; collapses after heavy drinking, becomes helpless "whimpering old idiot," dies during summer. **Chapter 18-19 transition**: Within three-to-four days of inheriting, Pitt determines to rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, reconcile with blood relations. **Chapter 19 (Autumn, fifth year)**: Briggs dismissed by Lady Southdown; Miss Crawley's legacies distributed; Bowls and Firkin receive legacies, marry, set up lodging-house in London. Rawdon and Rebecca visit Queen's Crawley for Sir Pitt's funeral ceremonies. Pitt comes to town in November to see lawyers, stays nearly a week in Curzon Street with Rawdon and Rebecca. **House renovation (November through Chapter 20)**: Determined upon Pitt's November arrival; Pitt's mansion in Great Gaunt Street bears mourning hatchment for late baronet but undergoes extensive renovation—black brick coating removed revealing cheerful blushing face streaked white, bronze knocker gilded, railings painted, becoming smartest house in quarter before green leaves replace yellow ones at Queen's Crawley. Work completed before winter; brothers' families agreed to meet at Christmas in country.
- **Year 1818 (referenced)**: Miss Osborne receives drawing lessons from Mr. Smee, portrait-painter and R.A.
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' Coffee-house, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham, Park Lane, Bond Street, Bayswater, Hyde Park, opera, Knightsbridge, nursery, parlour, ring, Times Office in City, Piccadilly, Bowls's lodging-house, Berkeley Square, Roehampton, Bloomsbury Square, Bedford Row, Upper Bedford Place, Bedford Square, Great Gaunt Street), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calaus, Dunkirk, Red Lion Square, Cursitor Street, Tooting, Gulton, Quenwick, Queen's Crawley, Clapham, Sugar-cane Lodge, Miremere, Valenciennes, Kensington Gardens, Hampshire, Madras, district chapel, tavern, Winchester Cathedral Close, Mudbury, Rectory, Parsonage, Hill farms of Mirecombe, Fuddleston, Southampton Gaol, Dunwick, Crawley Arms, Mudbury (saddler residence), Salwick harbour town, parsonage with lavender, May Fair, Chapel in May Fair, Cape Town, Finchley Common, Bryngate, India (station with gates of Commanding-Officer's compound, Colonel's house, guard-house, jackals in moonlight), Stillbrook (Lord Steyne's cottage).

## Main Characters

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley) (Chapters 19-20 – EXPANDED)**
- **Manipulation and cultivation of Pitt**: During November visit, Rebecca goes alone to greet Pitt at hotel, invites him to lodge at Curzon Street; her hospitalities described as irresistible through artless and frank warmth. She: bustles about his bedroom with coal-scuttle, makes him dinner while Rawdon dines out on business, cooks salmi of Lord Steyne's pheasants from Stillbrook cottage, serves white wine from Marquis of Steyne's cellars (claiming Rawdon picked it up cheaply from France, which is false), listens with "tenderest kindly interest" while hemming a shirt for little Rawdon, sings and coaxes him, creates blazing fire in drawing-room making it irresistible refuge from Gray's Inn lawyers. When departing, kisses hand from carriage, waves handkerchief, puts it to eyes once—performance moves Pitt emotionally; he broods that she "respected him" and that his wife Lady Jane is "mum and stupid" by comparison. Rebecca delicately hinted all these comparisons herself. **Financial manipulation**: When Pitt showed reluctance about money (grew "off and alarmed" at hints of embarrassments), Rebecca delicately tried ground and found it unsafe; Pitt launched long speech about straitened circumstances, tenants not paying, father's expenses, need to pay off incumbrances, and bankers overdrawn; Rebecca accepted very small sum for little Rawdon's benefit via check Pitt handed her. **Authority over house renovation**: Given full orders by Pitt to sell, barter, confiscate, or purchase furniture; oversees Miss Briggs and little Rawdon in superintending female band stitching blinds and hangings, rummaging through drawers and cupboards, taking inventories of china, glass, and properties.
- **Relationship with little Rawdon (Chapter 20 – CRITICAL NEW)**: During near two years (since early childhood), Rebecca has disliked her son, who bores and annoyed her. He suffered measles and hooping-cough. **Pivotal incident (Chapter 20)**: When little Rawdon crept downstairs attracted by sound of Rebecca singing to Lord Steyne, drawing room door suddenly opened, discovering child. Rebecca struck him on ears (boxes). Little Rawdon gasped "Why mayn't I hear her singing? Why don't she ever sing to me—as she does to that baldheaded man with the large teeth?" asking in rage and grief. Kitchen staff (cook, housemaid, footman) witnessed incident and judged Rebecca. After this incident, Rebecca's dislike increased to hatred; consciousness of child in house became reproach and pain to her; his very sight annoyed her; they were separated from that day of the boxes on the ear. Fear, doubt, and resistance sprang up in boy's own bosom.

**Sir Pitt Crawley (younger) – Baronet, MP (Chapters 19-20 – EXPANDED)**
- **November visit and emotional response**: Comes to town November to see lawyers; initially at hotel; Rebecca's invitation irresistible; lodges nearly week with Rawdon and Rebecca at Curzon Street. Passes happy evenings alone with Rebecca and Briggs. Appreciates Rebecca's salmi and wine from Steyne's cellars (wine brings "fire into the Baronet's pallid cheeks and a glow into his feeble frame"). **Emotional attachment**: Each day returns from Gray's Inn lawyers to Curzon Street's blazing fire with increasing gladness; feels "quite a pang at departing" when leaving. Watches Rebecca kiss hand from carriage, wave handkerchief, put it to eyes; pulls sealskin cap over his and broods that she respected him, that Rawdon is "foolish dull fellow" who doesn't appreciate her, that his own wife Lady Jane is "mum and stupid" compared to "brilliant little Becky." Agreed that house in London should be redecorated for next season and brothers' families should meet at Christmas in country.
- **Financial circumstances (Chapter 20)**: Pitt knows brother's family has nothing to live upon; aware he appropriated money that ought to have fallen to younger brother; feels "secret pangs of remorse" warning him he is morally Rawdon's debtor. When Rebecca delicately tried to obtain money for Rawdon's creditors, Pitt grew alarmed and launched long explanation of his own straitened circumstances: tenants won't pay, father's expenses involved him, wants to pay off incumbrances, bankers and agents overdrawn. Made compromise with Rebecca, giving small sum for little Rawdon's benefit. **Self-awareness**: Described as "just, decent man, not without brains, who said his prayers, and knew his catechism, and did his duty outwardly through life," yet morally aware something is due to Rawdon.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 20 – EXPANDED)**
- **Concern for creditors**: When Pitt departs, Rawdon says to Rebecca moodily he wishes he could have gotten money from Pitt; wants to give something to old Raggles, wishes old fellow not "kept out of all his money"; fears Raggles might let to somebody else. Rebecca reassures him, promises payment when Sir Pitt's affairs settled, gives him check from Pitt for little Rawdon's benefit. **Attachment to son**: Fondly attaches himself to little Rawdon; his "attachment towards the lad was curious too to witness."

**Little Rawdon (Son) (Chapters 19-20 – CRITICAL EXPANSION)**
- **Physical description (Chapter 20)**: Fine open-faced boy with blue eyes and waving flaxen hair; sturdy in limb; generous and soft in heart; about eight years old during events of Chapter 20.
- **Attachments (Chapter 20)**: Fondly attaches himself to all who are good to him: the pony, Lord Southdown (who gave the horse, causing boy to blush and glow when seeing him), the groom in charge of pony, Molly the cook (who gives ghost stories and good things from dinner), Miss Briggs (whom he plagues and laughs at), and especially his father Rawdon (whose affection for him is reciprocated). **Maternal rejection (Chapter 20 – CRITICAL)**: Beautiful mother-vision faded after while; during near two years Rebecca scarcely spoken to child; she disliked him; he had measles and hooping-cough; he bored her. **Pivotal traumatic incident (Chapter 20)**: Child crept downstairs attracted by Rebecca singing to Lord Steyne; drawing room door suddenly discovered him; Rebecca struck him on ears (boxes on the ear); little Rawdon gasped and sobbed, expressing in rage and grief: "Why mayn't I hear her singing? Why don't she ever sing to me—as she does to that baldheaded man with the large teeth?" Kitchen staff (cook, housemaid, footman) witnessed and judged Rebecca. **Aftermath**: Mother's dislike increased to hatred; consciousness of child in house became reproach and pain to her; his very sight annoyed her; fear, doubt, and resistance sprang up in boy's own bosom; separated from that day forward; ends his attachments around age eight.

**Miss Briggs (Chapters 19-20)**: No new developments; assists with house renovation and little Rawdon's daily oversight of Great Gaunt Street mansion.

**Major Dobbin (Chapter 19 – CRITICAL)**
- **Emotional crisis**: Upon reading Miss Dobbin's postscript revealing Amelia's impending marriage to Reverend Mr. Binny of Brompton, rushed from his house in moonlight with swift step and agitated countenance toward Colonel's bedchamber window—indicating profound emotional disturbance and unacknowledged deep attachment to Amelia despite denials of marriage intention weeks prior.

**Amelia Osborne (Chapter 19)**: Living in wretched place since bankruptcy; getting old with grey hair; about to marry Reverend Mr. Binny, curate of Brompton ("poor match"); described as CONSOLED; willing to give up son Georgy; maintains good spirits despite reduced fortune.

**Georgy (Chapter 19)**: Fine, handsome child; forward, saucy, self-willed; introduced to aunt Miss Osborne (pleased with him); hopes grandfather Mr. Osborne may relent; sent love to godpapa Dobbin.

**Lord Steyne (Chapters 19-20 – NEW)**: Owns Stillbrook cottage; provides pheasants for Rebecca's cooking; his wine (White Hermitage) from cellars given to Pitt; Rebecca sings to him in drawing room while little Rawdon listens from landing; described as "baldheaded man with the large teeth."

**Lord Southdown (Chapter 20)**: Kind young nobleman; gave little Rawdon a pony; boy blushes and glows when seeing him.

**Old Raggles (Chapter 20)**: Creditor or landlord of Rawdon and Rebecca; owed money; Rawdon wishes to pay him from Pitt's resources but Rebecca counsels patience until affairs settled.

**Cotho/Pebin Brackwood, Votho/Gamira Brackwood, Feena/Breena Stenworth, Nynelle Hollmere (Chapter 19-20)**: Minor figures with fragmentary mentions; names appear corrupted or uncertain in source material; discussed weather, harvest, lame horse; some letters burned; appear to inhabit Bryngate and Miremere area.

## Critical Facts
- **Rebecca's strategy with Pitt (Chapters 19-20)**: Through careful cultivation during November visit combining domestic arts (cooking), emotional performance (singing, hand-kissing, apparent tears at parting), flattery (suggesting he is "respected," superior to obtuse wife), and strategic vulnerability (hemming shirt for son), Rebecca has deeply moved Pitt emotionally while extracting minimal financial compensation. Her delicate insinuations about his wife's inferiority appear to have taken root. Agreement to decorate London house and meet at Christmas in country ensures continued contact.
- **Little Rawdon's psychological trauma (Chapter 20 – CRITICAL)**: Rejection by mother Rebecca during formative years (near two years of dislike) culminated in physical punishment (boxes on ear) when he sought her affection by listening to her sing to Lord Steyne. Public witnessing by kitchen staff (cook, housemaid, footman) compounds shame. Incident marks definitive break: mother's dislike becomes hatred; child develops fear and resistance; they are permanently separated emotionally and physically. Boy's attachments end around age eight, replaced by trauma.
- **Pitt's moral awareness and financial evasion (Chapter 20)**: Though described as just and decent man who knows his prayers and catechism, Pitt is acutely aware he is "morally Rawdon's debtor" yet actively evades financial restitution by pleading his own straitened circumstances (tenants not paying, father's expenses, incumbrances, overdrawn bankers). His discomfort at hints of money matters ("off and alarmed") suggests suppressed guilt about appropriating brother's rightful inheritance. Rebecca's delicate pressure proved "unsafe" ground—Pitt retreated into self-justification and minimal compensation.
- **Lord Steyne's presence (Chapters 19-20)**: Supplies luxury goods (pheasants, wine) to Rebecca; she sings to him in drawing room while little Rawdon yearns for her attention—suggesting developing relationship or seduction, and clear maternal preference for Steyne over her own son.
